messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Levi's Story

Levi Tanaka was sixty-seven when he came to therapy, though the lines around his eyes and the careful way he moved suggested someone older. He had spent forty years building a reputation as one of the finest interior designers in the Pacific Northwest, known for his meticulous eye and his ability to transform commercial spaces into environments that felt both intentional and alive. But for the past eighteen months, his practice had been dissolving. He no longer took on new projects. The studio he had maintained for three decades—a light-filled loft in Pioneer Square—sat mostly empty now.

The source of this collapse traced back to a single week in 2019, though Levi had only begun to understand its full weight in recent months. He had been in Syria then, part of a design consultation team brought in to advise on a luxury hotel renovation in Damascus. On the fourth day, the hotel where he and two colleagues were staying was seized during a period of intense factional conflict. What followed was seven days of confinement in a basement storage room with twelve other civilians—a space perhaps twelve feet by fifteen, lit by a single bulb, with a single door guarded from the outside. The men who held them shouted constantly, their voices in Arabic echoing off concrete walls, their demands and threats bleeding into one another. Levi, who spoke no Arabic, understood nothing of what was said, only the tone—the fury, the unpredictability. He remembered the smell of the room, the cold, the sound of boots on the stairs, the way his heart would accelerate at the slightest noise. On the sixth day, one of the guards had beaten another captive severely. On the seventh, they were released without explanation.

For the first year after his return, Levi had functioned. He had given statements to the State Department. He had seen a general practitioner who offered him a prescription for sleep. He had told himself that he was fortunate, that others had suffered far worse. But around month fourteen, something shifted. A client's voice—raised slightly in frustration during a Zoom call about a design revision—had triggered something in him that he could not control. His chest had tightened. He had felt certain, with a clarity that bypassed all rational thought, that he was in danger. The feeling had lasted for hours. After that, he found himself unable to return to the office. The thought of being in his studio—a space he loved, with windows overlooking the city—became unbearable. The studio was on the third floor. To reach it, he had to take an elevator. He had come to believe that enclosed spaces were fundamentally unsafe, that being in a room with a door that closed meant being trapped, that there was no difference between his studio and that basement in Damascus.

The avoidance had spread in concentric circles. He stopped taking meetings in person. Then he stopped scheduling meetings at all. His assistant, bewildered, had eventually taken another job. Two ongoing projects went to other designers. Clients who had worked with him for decades reached out, concerned, and Levi found himself unable to explain. When he tried to describe what had happened, the narrative would fragment. He could see the room clearly—the exact shade of the concrete, the way the light fell—but when he tried to articulate why he could no longer work, the words would dissolve. He would find himself unable to finish a sentence, unable to explain the connection between a basement in Damascus and a design studio in Seattle.

What frightened him most was a feeling he could not quite name. When he was in any enclosed space—even his own bedroom—his body would respond before his mind could catch up. His breathing would shallow. His muscles would tense. He felt safest only when he was in open rooms with his back against a wall, where he could see the whole space, where no one could approach from behind. In crowded places, he would position himself so he could monitor the exits and the other people in the room. He had rehearsed conversations endlessly before they happened, imagining every possible response, every way things could go wrong. But no amount of mental rehearsal seemed to help.

What made him finally seek help was his daughter's wedding, scheduled for next spring. She lived in Boston. She had asked him to walk her down the aisle. The ceremony was to be held in a church—a space with a single entrance, pews that would be full of people, nowhere to position himself safely. The thought of it had triggered the kind of panic he had not experienced in months. He sat in his living room, in the corner where his back was against two walls, and wept. He did not want to miss his daughter's wedding. He did not want to be the man who could not walk his daughter down the aisle because he was afraid of a room.
